articleTitle: The what, how and why of intellectual property
abstract: The author presents an overview of intellectual property by examining: confidentiality; copyright; trade marks; registered design; design right; patents; ownership; licensing; and legal infringements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

The author outlines how Vosper Thornycroft (UK) Ltd. and the Department of Mechanical Engineering of University College London, supported by the Teaching Company Scheme, have co-operated over a period of four years to create a computer based system for the concept design of ships. This system, known as CASCADES (Computer Aided Ship Concept And Design Evaluation System), is based on research and development previously carried out separately at VT and UCL, and is now in operation at both establishments. It is being used for improved concept exploration by VT and for training Naval Architecture students at UCL. This is an example of technology transfer between an academic institution and an industrial partner which has been mutually beneficial to both parties.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

It is a cliche that in the UK we are less successful than our competitors at translating our inventions into successful commercial products. Here, the author argues that we must not allow prophets of doom and sensationalist headlines to detract from our achievements; on many fronts, we are getting technology transfer right. He illustrates the mechanisms for technology transfer using examples of several success stories.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vibration measurement instrument using laser Doppler holography
abstract: Historically the Rover test technology group has researched and developed optical based measurement techniques. Optical methods offer several advantages over classical techniques: the measurement is made in a noncontacting manner and therefore the mass and stiffness of the structure are not changed, very good measurement resolution is possible by utilising laser light, while field data can be acquired instantaneously using holographic or photographic techniques. In particular TV holography has been found to give real time, whole field measurements of the vibration and deformation of structures. However, the technology is complex and sufficiently unknown to structural engineers such that a significant barrier exists in transferring this technology to them. Therefore a series of projects have been undertaken to 'de-skill' the technology, thus enabling its transfer. The authors describe the problems in transferring holographic technology and the technological developments undertaken which address this issue.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
